title: Matrices as transformations of space
summary: A linear transformation moves every point of the plane while keeping grid lines straight, parallel and evenly spaced, with the origin fixed. Because of that, where î and ĵ land decides everything, and a matrix is just those two landing spots written as columns. Multiplying a matrix by [x, y] means taking x copies of the first column plus y copies of the second.
llm_link: A layer of a language model holds a weight matrix W. Multiplying an embedding x by W moves it to a new place in a (possibly different-sized) space; column j of W is where input direction j is sent. Training is a search for matrices that move token vectors to useful places.
key_ideas: Linear transformation: grid lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced, and the origin stays put.
So if v = x·î + y·ĵ, then T(v) = x·T(î) + y·T(ĵ): the recipe survives the move.
The matrix lists where î lands as its first column and where ĵ lands as its second column.
Matrix times vector, column picture: [[a, b], [c, d]] · [x, y] = x·[a, c] + y·[b, d]. The row-by-row rule gives the same numbers.
Examples: [[0, −1], [1, 0]] turns the plane a quarter circle; [[1, 1], [0, 1]] is a shear; columns on one line flatten the plane onto that line (their span).

quiz.q: A transformation sends î to (3, 1) and ĵ to (0, 2). What is its matrix?
quiz.explain: Columns are landing spots: first column (3, 1), second column (0, 2). Written as rows, that is [[3, 0], [1, 2]].

quiz.q: Which matrix turns the plane a quarter circle counter-clockwise?
quiz.explain: A quarter turn sends î (pointing right) to (0, 1) (up) and ĵ (up) to (−1, 0) (left). Those are the columns: [[0, −1], [1, 0]].

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a linear transformation?
quiz.explain: Adding 1 moves the origin to (1, 0), and a linear transformation must keep the origin fixed. The others keep grid lines straight, parallel and evenly spaced with the origin in place.

quiz.q: A layer computes y = W x for an embedding x. What does column j of W tell you?
options: The j-th word of the vocabulary
Where the j-th input direction (the j-th basis vector) is sent
quiz.explain: Exactly as with î and ĵ: column j is W applied to the j-th basis vector, so y is x₁·(column 1) + x₂·(column 2) + …, a combination of the columns weighted by the input.

problems.title: Matrix times vector, by columns
problems.prompt:
A matrix is stored as a list of rows: M = [[2, -1], [1, 1]]. Its columns are where the basis vectors land.

Write matvec(M, v) using the column picture: start with a zero vector and add v[j] copies of column j for every j. It should work for any number of rows and columns, as long as len(v) equals the number of columns.

matvec([[2, -1], [1, 1]], [2, 1])   # [3, 3]
matvec([[0, -1], [1, 0]], [1, 0])   # [0, 1]  (quarter turn sends i-hat up)

If the sizes do not fit, raise a ValueError.
problems.starter:
def column(M, j):
    """Column j of M (a list of rows)."""
    return [row[j] for row in M]


def matvec(M, v):
    n_rows, n_cols = len(M), len(M[0])
    # TODO 1: raise ValueError if len(v) != n_cols

    result = [0] * n_rows
    # TODO 2: for each j, add v[j] copies of column(M, j) to result

    return result

tests.name: i-hat comes out as the first column
tests.code:
out = matvec([[2, -1], [1, 1]], [1, 0])
assert out == [2, 1], f'M times i-hat is where i-hat lands, the first column (2, 1); got {out}. Are you taking columns, not rows?'

tests.name: quarter turn
tests.code:
out = matvec([[0, -1], [1, 0]], [1, 0])
assert out == [0, 1], f'a quarter turn sends i-hat (right) to (0, 1) (up); got {out}'

tests.name: rejects a size mismatch

hints: if len(v) != n_cols: raise ValueError("vector length must equal the number of columns")

problems.title: Build a matrix from where i-hat and j-hat land
problems.prompt:
Write matrix_from(i_lands, j_lands) that returns the 2×2 matrix (as a list of rows) whose first column is i_lands and second column is j_lands.

matrix_from([2, 1], [-1, 1])   # [[2, -1], [1, 1]]

Careful: the landing spots are columns, but the matrix is stored as rows.

tests.name: the example from the video
tests.code:
out = matrix_from([2, 1], [-1, 1])
assert out == [[2, -1], [1, 1]], f'expected [[2, -1], [1, 1]], got {out}. If you got [[2, 1], [-1, 1]], you stored the landing spots as rows instead of columns.'

tests.name: quarter turn
tests.code:
out = matrix_from([0, 1], [-1, 0])
assert out == [[0, -1], [1, 0]], f'i-hat lands on (0, 1) and j-hat on (-1, 0), so the matrix is [[0, -1], [1, 0]]; got {out}'

tests.name: identity
tests.code:
out = matrix_from([1, 0], [0, 1])
assert out == [[1, 0], [0, 1]], f'if nothing moves, the matrix is the identity [[1, 0], [0, 1]]; got {out}'

hints: Row 0 is [i_lands[0], j_lands[0]] and row 1 is [i_lands[1], j_lands[1]].
problems.solution:
def matrix_from(i_lands, j_lands):
    return [[i_lands[0], j_lands[0]], [i_lands[1], j_lands[1]]]

problems.title: Transform a whole shape (NumPy)
problems.prompt:
NumPy multiplies a matrix by many points at once if you put the points side by side as columns of a 2×n array. Then M @ pts transforms every column.

Write transform(M, pts) where M is a 2×2 NumPy array and pts is a 2×n array; return the transformed 2×n array.

Then write rotation(degrees) returning the 2×2 matrix of a counter-clockwise rotation. Where does î land after turning by θ? At (cos θ, sin θ). And ĵ? At (−sin θ, cos θ). Those are the columns. (Use np.radians.)

square = np.array([[0, 1, 1, 0],
                   [0, 0, 1, 1]])   # four corners, one per column
transform(rotation(90), square)  # ≈ [[0, 0, -1, -1], [0, 1, 1, 0]]

tests.name: shape is kept
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out = transform(np.array([[2, -1], [1, 1]]), np.zeros((2, 5)))
assert out is not None, 'transform returned None'
assert out.shape == (2, 5), f'2x2 @ 2x5 gives 2x5, got {out.shape}'

tests.name: the example from the video
tests.code:
import numpy as np
M = np.array([[2, -1], [1, 1]])
out = transform(M, np.array([[1, 0, 2], [0, 1, 1]]))
assert np.allclose(out, [[2, -1, 3], [1, 1, 3]]), f'columns should become (2, 1), (-1, 1) and (3, 3); got {out.tolist()}'

tests.name: rotation(90) sends i-hat up
tests.code:
import numpy as np
R = rotation(90)
assert np.allclose(R, [[0, -1], [1, 0]]), f'a quarter turn is [[0, -1], [1, 0]], got {np.round(R, 3).tolist()}'

tests.name: rotating the unit square
tests.code:
import numpy as np
sq = np.array([[0, 1, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1, 1]])
out = transform(rotation(90), sq)
assert np.allclose(out, [[0, 0, -1, -1], [0, 1, 1, 0]]), f'got {np.round(out, 3).tolist()}'

tests.name: rotation keeps lengths
tests.code:
import numpy as np
p = np.array([[3.0], [4.0]])
out = transform(rotation(37), p)
assert abs(np.linalg.norm(out) - 5) < 1e-9, f'a rotation should not change the length 5, got {np.linalg.norm(out)}'

hints: transform is one line: return M @ pts
np.array([[np.cos(t), -np.sin(t)], [np.sin(t), np.cos(t)]]): rows here, but read it by columns: (cos t, sin t) and (-sin t, cos t).
